📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.

It has been revealed that this is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

Sources indicate that in this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

Recent findings suggest that we've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

Recent findings suggest that but swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

Sources indicate that we'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

Industry observers note that A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

Industry observers note that this creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Recent findings suggest that agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:.

A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

In a recent development, A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:.

Industry observers note that the team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

In a recent development, the main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:.

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

According to recent reports, for every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

Sources indicate that in TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

In a recent development, over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

Recent findings suggest that the team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

Sources indicate that the team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:.

Industry observers note that that is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

It has been revealed that no agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:.

It has been revealed that with eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each upgrade generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts promptly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:.

Sources indicate that the figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

Recent findings suggest that one TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

Sources indicate that this shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

Industry observers note that to run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-patch 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

According to recent reports, once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

Recent findings suggest that this first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

#229799. Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.
  • Sources indicate that now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference.
  • Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Sources indicate that now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

In a recent development, this latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:.

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create latest variations for a target document type or language.

According to recent reports, figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry.

Recent findings suggest that we trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

Recent findings suggest that we then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

Recent findings suggest that A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

It has been revealed that figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison reveals the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Industry observers note that figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 reveals three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:.

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass.

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

Sources indicate that in the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

It has been revealed that the worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

It has been revealed that figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

In a recent development, figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

In a recent development, to adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

Breaking: Why a microtonal MIDI clip changes pitch on another computer

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (218 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, written autonomously by an AI assistant for the Sonari team.
  • A collaborator loads your MIDI clip, sees the notes you expected, and hears a different chord.
  • Take MIDI note 69 as A at 440 Hz, and compare two ways to interpret a major third above it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, written autonomously by an AI assistant for the Sonari team. The Python example is synthetic; it does not test a Sonari or Ableton export.

A collaborator loads your MIDI clip, sees the notes you expected, and hears a different chord. Before moving any notes, check whether the file carried the tuning or just the note numbers.

Take MIDI note 69 as A at 440 Hz, and compare two ways to interpret a major third above it. With a 5:4 ratio the upper pitch is 550 Hz (386.314 cents up). With twelve-tone equal temperament the upper pitch is 554.37 Hz (400 cents up). In this illustration either mapping can associate the upper pitch with note 73. The note number cannot tell you which mapping the sender heard.

Industry observers note that run this Python 3 example to generate two synthetic WAVs. Both use the same root, level and duration; only the upper frequency changes. Start playback at a low level.

Industry observers note that if the receiver only uses equal temperament, the WAV is the reliable way to hear your original pitch choices. Live can also approximate a tuned clip using its Retune Set option, but it may move or drop notes. Do it in a copy and label the approximation.

Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (391 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face.
  • Industry observers note that local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve.
  • Recent findings suggest that you can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Industry observers note that local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

Recent findings suggest that you can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard reveals two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:.

In a recent development, both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

Industry observers note that we benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Industry observers note that standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

--network mainnet matters. In mppx 0.22.1, if you omit --network and do not set a custom RPC URL, funding/account helpers default to testnet. Our live challenges are mainnet (chainId: 4217). Pass the flag.

#229789. Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month.
  • Sources indicate that with five days left, I allowed myself a little fun.
  • I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

Sources indicate that with five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

According to recent reports, for CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX claims makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:.

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:.

A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Industry observers note that making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

According to recent reports, the payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

According to recent reports, on the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no initiative to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

According to recent reports, most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

Three issues were never explained: the transformer compiled as one graph returned NaN at one size, the first shot that ends on keyframes was slow in each new process (even with every graph in the cache), and the latent upsampler fails to load next to the transformer, so it stays on the CPU.

Some of this is being fixed upstream. diffusers#15420 (open) fixes the LTX-2 pipelines, which would make the second workaround above unnecessary. diffusers#14725 (still open) brings tensor and context parallelism into one ParallelConfig, and a _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned.

On the performance side, once the models are loaded, a 10-second 2048×1024 clip with sound takes 22 to 23 s. That rivals LTX's paid API, on half of the instance. A service would keep its processes up, as they take about 3 minutes to load the models, and 80 s for their first clip.

On the feature side, diffusers has what it takes to draft a movie. The shots come from prompts, and keep their subject from one shot to the next by starting or ending on frames of other shots. Takes differ by their seed, and the film file keeps the one I picked. Re-run with the same code and film file, and you get the same film back, byte for byte. A shot can also start from an image, such as a storyboard frame or a character sheet, which the condition pipeline takes the same way as frames (I did not try it in a film).

LTX calls LTX-2.5 a world model, with robotics as an emerging use. Robots, cars and drones learn from videos of what their cameras see, and a world model can make more of them, including events too rare or too risky to film. So I also tried it on real footage, with the same code: a shot can start from the first second of a real camera clip and invent what happens next. One frame was not enough, as the model cannot tell from it how fast things move.

Recent findings suggest that here is the head camera of a Fourier GR1-T2 humanoid robot (a clip from NVIDIA's GR1-100), looking down at a table. In the real 6-second clip, the robot's left hand picks an orange from a plate and drops it in a tray. The model only sees the first second of that clip (the hands raised, before anything moves) and invents the rest. What really happened, next to its invention:.

Same scene, same pick: the model invents the grab on its own, and keeps the table, the hands and the fruit consistent with the real footage. More interesting are the events that did not happen. From the same second, with only the prompt changed, a person leans over and grabs the orange too, and the human hand and the robot hand carry it to the tray together. Five takes, with the real footage first:.

Recent findings suggest that the person's gestures and timing differ in each take, and the robot's arm adapts to them. That is the appeal for training: not one continuation of a clip, but a distribution of them, each reproducible from its film file and seed.

The robotics folder of the bucket has the five takes with their JSON files, and a second example from the front camera of a car in a snowstorm (Boreas), where the alternate event is slush thrown on the lens by a passing truck. Asked to make the car accelerate instead, the model kept its speed: the prompt does not override what the first second of footage already implies.

In a recent development, these videos follow prompts, not the robot's or car's commands: a training setup would need generation conditioned on those actions. For that, a team fine-tunes the pre-trained checkpoint of LTX-2.5 on the frames and actions of its own robots.

The Ferrari made it around the track, on half of its cylinders.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers customers to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.IntroductionLimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely newly introduced entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). Hi everyone, Seb and Jan here 👋!

It has been revealed that this week, Ricky Hanlon leaves Meta after 8 years on React. React Router fixed 7 vulnerabilities, and an automated React2STEAL campaign is leaking secrets from unpatched React and Next.js servers. TanStack Query shared its v6 roadmap. Next.js is experimenting with a Go server.

On mobile, Reanimated 4.8 makes Shared Element Transitions stable. An RFC proposes a platform-agnostic React Native core, to make out-of-tree platforms easier to maintain. Skia and WebGPU now download their prebuilt binaries at build time, which makes the npm packages much lighter.

Sources indicate that elsewhere, next week's TC39 meeting could move Import Text to stage 4. Firefox 161 unlocks CSS random() in all browsers. Parcel 3 can now build static sites on its own. Node.js is preparing to enable pointer compression by default.

According to recent reports, fewer findings. Only real risks.

In a recent development, AI-generated code can introduce vulnerabilities that are easy to miss in a pull request. CodeRabbit Security continuously reviews your codebase for complex bugs and security risks, using full-codebase context to follow data flows, dependencies, and patterns beyond the latest diff.

Run CodeRabbit Security on your own repositories today.

Sentry Metrics Workshop: See the Why Behind App Changes.

Recent findings suggest that 📊 Sentry is hosting a live workshop on how to instrument Sentry Application Metrics (along with traces, logs, and errors) to track the signals that matter, with the context you need to get to the root cause. Then turn your metrics into dashboards and alerts to make your life easier.

👉 Save your seat for December 10.

Reanimated 4.8 - Shared Element Transitions stable.

One of the most anticipated features is finally stable, and enabled by default! Tag two views with the same sharedTransitionTag, put them in two components, and when the target boundary becomes active, the view travels to it. Think of an album cover moving from a song list into the now-playing screen. It's a small detail, but it makes transitions feel much more natural.

It has been revealed that transitions are no longer tied to navigation, so they also work between tabs, or between two views on the same screen. The moving view is the actual view, not a snapshot, so its content keeps running during the transition. On iOS, it even follows your finger during a swipe-back gesture. When the two views have different children, the newly introduced SharedTransition.fadeContent() modifier fades them out and in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, go-intl is a high-performance internationalization library with a simpler API. It should be the definitive answer to internationalization in Go.

I decided to write go-intl while I was building the terminal and desktop clients for a personal agent entirely in Go. When I needed to add internationalization, I took one look at go-i18n’s API and knew it wasn’t what I wanted. I wanted something simpler, so I decided to build a upcoming library with better performance and a simpler API.

If you find this article useful, give go-intl a star ✨. If you have any questions, feel free to open an issue.

A high-performance Go internationalization library with a simple API for sharing translations across terminal, desktop, and server applications.

Pick a language once, then translate by key.

A Bubble Tea model, a MyGo window, an NSGo view, a Wails app’s local Go backend, and an HTTP handler can each select a language from the same immutable catalog.

Apple M3 Pro, Go 1.27.1 (darwin/arm64). The ten interpolation cases use medians from the six-run v0.1.1 comparison. The two static lookups and the English plural retain the original three-run medians. Each cell reports ns/op · B/op · allocs/op. Speedup is go-i18n time divided by go-intl time.

v0.1.1 benchmark results · Original benchmarks and methodology.

The core package requires Go 1.25 or later. To try the example in….

Here are the full benchmark results. Overall, go-intl beats go-i18n by a wide margin on translation speed, bytes allocated, and number of allocations.

Measured on an Apple M3 Pro with Go 1.27.1 (darwin/arm64).

go-intl supports five sources for translations.

go-intl supports the following message syntax.

You can use go-intl with Bubble Tea, in a local Wails backend, in a Go web backend, and with mygo or nsgo. That covers terminal apps, desktop apps, and backend services.

According to recent reports, by the way, Go is the best language for the AI era. It runs fast, compiles fast, and gives AI fast feedback. You should use Go. Go is all you need.

Let’s look at the thinking behind the design.

Industry observers note that imagine a page with forty pieces of text to translate. Three of them are a status label, a greeting, and the number of items in a cart.

All three are strings, but each is produced differently. Ready is already written out in the translation file. Hello, Ada! needs interpolation to fill in the user’s name. And 7 items depends on the quantity to determine whether to use item or items.

Walking through how these three strings are produced shows where go-intl saves time.

Suppose an app provides English and Simplified Chinese translations. The same key gives different text in each language.

From here on, a dictionary means one set of translations. It holds the message keys and their translations for a given language. Look up screen.ready in the English dictionary and you get Ready. Look it up in the Chinese dictionary and you get 就绪.

Before you can look up a key, you need to know which dictionary to open.

Say the browser sends this Accept-Language header.

Sources indicate that the browser prefers American English, followed by English, then Simplified Chinese. The app has no separate en-US dictionary, but it does provide en, so it can select the English dictionary.

This is language matching. The app compares the languages the user prefers with the ones it offers and picks a suitable match.

With English selected, screen.ready resolves to Ready.

With both dictionaries loaded into a go-i18n bundle, a caller can translate two labels like this.

Recent findings suggest that newLocalizer reads those language preferences. Here’s its implementation.

Industry observers note that parseTags(langs) parses the input into language tags and stores them in tags. At this point, what the Localizer holds is the browser’s list of preferences. The quality weights (q=0.9 and q=0.8) determine the order. For this header, the localizer holds the following preferences.

Industry observers note that dictionary selection happens later. Each call to Localize or MustLocalize reaches getMessageTemplate, which starts with these three lines.

The first line matches the preferences, the second retrieves the supported tag, and the third looks up the message for that language. Suppose bundle.tags is [zh-CN, en]. When we look up screen.ready, the matcher returns i = 1. We read bundle.tags[1], which is en, then look up screen.ready in the English messages. When we look up screen.cancel, loc.tags still holds the same three tags. The matcher runs again, returns i = 1 again, and we look up screen.cancel in English. The calls share the browser’s preference list. Each call works out which language to use.

In a recent development, that’s two language matches for two labels. Translate all forty labels with this localizer and the matcher runs forty times.

Industry observers note that within this request, the browser’s preferences stay the same and so do the dictionaries. Both lookups will pick English.

It has been revealed that go-intl lets the app make that choice at the start of the request and reuse it for later translations. Suppose catalog already contains our two dictionaries and English is the default.

catalog.Match(header) picks English and returns a locale that remembers the choice. The t created from that locale uses the English dictionary directly on later calls, without processing the browser’s preferences again.

That’s what it means to bind a dictionary. The translator remembers which dictionary to look in on subsequent calls. It only needs a reference to the existing data, so there’s no need to copy the English translations.

It has been revealed that A language may be missing a message. If Chinese is selected and has no entry for screen.cancel, the lookup should try the default English dictionary next. go-intl builds that fallback order when it loads the catalog. Locale.chain holds the resulting sequence of dictionary indexes.

It takes just a few lines in catalog.go to store the result of that choice.

Here’s an example of what locale contains after catalog.Match returns.

Recent findings suggest that A lookup starts with the first dictionary in that sequence. Here’s the part of lookup that handles a hit there.

In a recent development, keys is a Go map from message keys to integer indexes. programs[idx] holds the message at that index. For Ready, the stored text is already the finished string, so it can be returned directly.

If the page’s keys all start with screen., you can leave that prefix out of individual calls.

screen is a namespace, a prefix shared by a group of messages. It has its own short-key index, so the translator can look up ready directly without constructing screen.ready first. At load time, go-intl splits each key at its last dot. For screen.ready, that gives us the namespace screen and the short key ready. If this message is at index 7, both entries point to the same compiled message.

At translation time, the scoped translator uses the index stored in Locale.direct.

Sources indicate that the short-key index gives you a simpler way to call the translator, with no performance gain. A translator that takes full keys can reuse the selected language just as well. The static benchmarks below use full keys.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. All the translations on a page can share one language match.

Once you’ve found Ready, you can display it directly. Once you’ve found Hello, {first}!, you still need to replace {first} with the name.

Sources indicate that A message with a slot for a value is a template. go-i18n uses Go’s text/template syntax, so its version of the greeting is Hello, {{.first}}!.

Three things happen in sequence.

Change Ada to Grace and the structure stays the same. The greeting still has a prefix, a name, and an exclamation mark. Only the output needs to be built again.

Sources indicate that in go-i18n, TextParser.Parse in i18n/template/text_parser.go creates the template. At this point the delimiters and options are already in place.

Sources indicate that .Parse(src) parses Hello, {{.first}}! into a Go template, which go-i18n wraps in a parsedTextTemplate.

Recent findings suggest that plain text gets a shorter path. Before creating a Go template, the parser looks for the opening delimiter, which defaults to {{.

Ready contains no {{, so the parser keeps the original string and skips the Go template parser.

The cache lives in internal/template.go. The default parser allows caching when there are no custom template functions. Here’s Template.Execute.

On the first call for this message, parseOnce.Do runs parser.Parse and stores the result in t.parsedTemplate. Later calls pick up that result and pass the current data to pt.Execute(data).

When go-i18n displays Ready again, it can reuse the cached result. When it displays the greeting again, it reuses the parsed template as well. The difference in static lookup times comes from the steps that lead up to finding the message, including language selection and the lookup itself.

Sources indicate that in go-intl v0.1.0, greetings such as Hello, {first}! were already parsed when the dictionary was loaded. Each time the greeting was displayed, the general-purpose renderer still had to loop over the prefix, the name, and the exclamation mark in order. v0.1.1 built on that implementation to speed up interpolation. Since the compiler already knows where the name goes, it stores the argument name along with the concatenation order.

Sources indicate that we tested both versions and go-i18n with the same three inputs on an Apple M3 Pro running Go 1.27.1. We prepared the argument map ahead of time and took the median of six runs for each case. Each cell gives nanoseconds per call · heap allocations per call.

Take the greeting in the second row. Filling in the same name went from 80.1 ns to 54.4 ns, and from three heap allocations to two. To see what changed, look at what each version keeps in memory for that greeting.

Recent findings suggest that suppose the English dictionary has just one message. Both versions load it the same way.

Industry observers note that at load time, compileMessage parses "Hello, {first}!". It’s the only message, so keys["screen.hello"] is 0 and the compiled result goes in programs[0]. We already know the argument is called first. We’ll get the actual name when someone calls the translator.

Industry observers note that an instruction is a Go struct. Its kind tells the renderer how to interpret text. With opText, it writes the text as given. With opValue, it uses the text as an argument name.

Now bind t := catalog.Translations("en") and call t("screen.hello", intl.Values{"first": "Ada"}). The first instruction writes "Hello, " to a strings.Builder. The second looks up "first" and writes "Ada" to the same builder. The third writes "!". Pass a different name and the renderer walks the same three instructions again.

If we spell out the successful path through (*messageRender).body in message_render.go, it amounts to this.

The parser starts with the same three instructions. The compiler sees only literal text and ordinary placeholders, so it pairs each argument with the literal text immediately before it. Two structs hold the result.

Sources indicate that the "Hello, " from the first instruction and the "first" from the second now share an entry. The "!" from the third goes in suffix. Pass in "Ada" again and the renderer only has to read args[0], look up its key in the argument map, and concatenate the prefix, name, and suffix. Both versions look up values["first"] exactly once. v0.1.1 saves the work of interpreting two literal-text instructions and writing the pieces to a builder on every call.

compileInterpolation in message.go builds the plain field at load time.

It has been revealed that each opValue marks a placeholder. literalText collects the text since the previous placeholder, and that becomes the new argument’s prefix. Whatever follows the last argument becomes the suffix.

Here, “compiling” means putting the message into a form that’s easy to use later. To produce the greeting, the renderer just looks up the value by its argument name and joins the pieces.

If the value is already a string, messageString returns it directly. Otherwise, it converts the value to a string and returns that.

A message with one argument reaches these lines at the end of interpolation.render.

For the greeting, the result is "Hello, " + "Ada" + "!". For a message that consists entirely of {first}, both surrounding strings are empty. The renderer can return "Ada" itself.

Sources indicate that go-i18n hands the greeting to the Go template executor. Here’s the execution code in i18n/template/text_parser.go.

These benchmarks pass the same map[string]any{"first": "Ada"} to both libraries. go-i18n also accepts a struct as TemplateData. Even with the template cached, Go’s text/template has to decide how to read {{.first}} each time it executes. It first looks for a method with that name, then uses reflection to distinguish a struct from a map. Here the input is a map, so the executor uses MapIndex to read "first" and writes "Ada" to the buffer along with the surrounding text. Field evaluation in Go’s template executor.

go-intl defines named arguments as type Values map[string]any. At load time it records "first" in arg.key. At execution time values[arg.key] reads the map directly, so the renderer can skip checking the container type and looking up the value through reflection. The value itself is still any, so messageString checks whether it’s a string. Here it gets "Ada", which can go straight into the concatenation.

Sources indicate that go-i18n’s default template uses text/template.(*state).evalField. Here receiver is the object being read, and fieldName is "first". The excerpt shows the struct and map branches after the method lookup. Comments mark the omitted code. Go standard library source.

For ordinary interpolation, go-intl uses (*interpolation).render. The same name is already stored in arg.key. Inside the loop over the placeholders, these lines look up the value and turn it into text.

Figure 2. Caching avoids parsing the template again. When the message is simple enough, its execution can be shortened as well.

Now consider a message with sixteen placeholders.

According to recent reports, the keys run from v00 through v15. If we kept doing result = result + next, each concatenation could copy everything accumulated so far. The longer the message, the more often we’d copy its opening bytes.

For ordinary placeholders, go-intl starts with a local [128]byte array. It appends literals and argument values in order, then builds the final string. Here’s the full implementation in message_render.go.

The first fifteen values go into the buffer. The sixteenth goes straight into the final concatenation, saving a trip through the buffer.

It has been revealed that each value here is three bytes. The first fifteen values and the fourteen slashes between them occupy 15 × 3 + 14 = 59 bytes. They all fit in the same local array.

Sources indicate that through the public API, this case took three heap allocations per call in go-intl and 37 in go-i18n. The final string still needs storage. Longer arguments can also push append past the capacity of the local array and force it to grow the buffer.

Industry observers note that if the same argument appears sixteen times, go-intl still reads it sixteen times in order. An argument can implement String(), and successive calls can produce different results, so each occurrence is evaluated separately. The occurrences share the space used to hold intermediate text.

It has been revealed that while working on general-purpose interpolation, I also tried filling a string slice with the pieces and then calling strings.Join(parts, "") to produce the translation. For {first}/{last}/{id}, the filled slice is []string{"", "Ada", "/", "Lovelace", "/", "42", ""}. Three values and four literals take up seven slots. The empty strings at the beginning and end each take a slot, too.

It has been revealed that scale that up to sixteen placeholders separated by slashes. There are fifteen slashes between the values, and the slice still keeps an empty string before the first value and after the last.

Figure 2a. Sixteen values have fifteen separators between them. With the two empty pieces at the ends, that makes 33 slots.

According to recent reports, I ran this experiment on an Apple M3 Pro (darwin/arm64) with Go 1.27.1. Each argument value was three ASCII bytes, with slashes between placeholders. I bound the translation function and prepared the arguments before starting the timer. Each timed call produced one translation. The table gives the median of six runs with -cpu=1 and 250 ms per case per run.

Repeating one argument sixteen times also takes 33 slots. Each occurrence still contributes its own value to the slice. Both sixteen-placeholder cases used 648 bytes across three heap allocations per translation.

A cart label needs more than a number in a fixed sentence. In English, a cart with one item reads 1 item. A cart with seven reads 7 items.

It has been revealed that figure 2b. For an English cart count, 1 selects one. Every other nonnegative integer selects other.

Here’s the cart message in go-intl.

It has been revealed that count is the number of items in the cart. one and other are English plural categories. Inside either branch, # stands for the count to display.

At load time, compileMessage parses the cart message into its code slice. The body of one occupies indexes 2 and 3. The body of other occupies indexes 5 and 6. We can already say what each branch will write. Which one runs depends on the count supplied at translation time.

Industry observers note that when the parser reaches the closing brace of one, the slice has four instructions. It sets code[1].end to 4, the first position past that branch. Here that position happens to be the label for other. By the time the parser closes other, the slice has seven instructions. Index 7 is also the end of the whole plural block.

It has been revealed that compileMessage turns the input string into a sequence of steps the renderer can follow. If you’ve studied compilers, two familiar ideas can help here. One is a grammar, a set of rules describing how sentences in a language can be formed. The other is nesting.

At translation time, the renderer uses those indexes to run the chosen branch.

Industry observers note that follow a call with count = 7. The outer loop has read opPlural at index 0 and advanced i to 1. r.choose(1, op, 7) starts checking labels there. English puts 7 in other, whose label is at index 4, so branch is 4. This message has no plural offset, so adjusted, the value for #, is still 7.

According to recent reports, the recursive call is now r.body(b, 5, 7, 7). The first two numbers describe the half-open instruction range [5, 7). The last is the quantity. Instruction 5 writes "7" into b. Instruction 6 appends " items". The result is "7 items".

With a count of 1, it’s easier to see what the last line, i = op.end, does. The body of one occupies indexes 2 and 3. After writing "1 item", the outer loop jumps straight to index 7, skipping the other branch.

Sources indicate that if the author adds =7 {Exactly seven}, a count of exactly 7 takes that branch ahead of other. The renderer still checks candidate labels, but the recorded boundaries let it skip their bodies.

After selecting # items, we still need text for #.

Sources indicate that for the integer 7 in English, strconv.Itoa(7) gives us exactly "7". With 12345, English normally calls for a grouping separator, as in 12,345. Other languages may also use different digit shapes.

localizedNumber uses strconv.Itoa only when the two forms are known to agree.

In a recent development, the conditions are narrow. The format must be an ordinary number, the dictionary language must be en or en-US, and the value must be a Go int between −999 and 999 inclusive.

In a recent development, the 7 in 7 items qualifies. Other cases go through the locale-aware number printer. Each dictionary gets its printer when the catalog is built and reuses it across calls.

The go-i18n benchmark uses the same message ID, screen.items. In its English dictionary, One holds {{.PluralCount}} item and Other holds {{.PluralCount}} items. Here’s the call.

The two occurrences of 7 are used in different places. go-i18n first reads cfg.PluralCount to prepare the value its plural rule needs. As before, the Localizer calls l.bundle.matcher.Match(l.tags...) to select the English dictionary, then looks up "screen.items". The English rule puts the first 7 in Other, so it selects {{.PluralCount}} items. At this point, all it has done is choose the template. The template still has to run, as we saw in the interpolation section. That’s one reason go-i18n is slower here.

Sources indicate that in go-intl, English was bound before the call. Once other is selected, the renderer already has the integer 7 for that branch. opPound writes "7", then opText appends " items".

In a recent development, figure 3. Choosing the wording and formatting the number are two separate steps, each with its own input and output.

Now we can return to the benchmarks and connect each row to the steps we’ve just walked through.

ns/op is the time per operation in nanoseconds. Allocations are also counted per operation. Speedup is the go-i18n time divided by the go-intl time.

Sources indicate that the static cases use full keys and a translator bound with locale.Translations(). The 12.9 ns result uses no screen namespace or short-key index. Both libraries recorded zero heap allocations, so the timing difference lies in the work they do to find and return the same text.

In a CPU profile of go-i18n repeatedly looking up one key, language matching accounted for 64% of the samples, the largest single cost. Even removing it entirely, with everything else held constant, would give a theoretical speedup of about 1 / (1 − 0.64) ≈ 2.8×. The roughly ninefold difference in the table reflects the two lookup paths as a whole.

Industry observers note that the greeting uses direct concatenation for ordinary placeholders. The sixteen-field case shows the benefit of sharing a temporary buffer. A message index has one job. Given a string key, it returns the message index. I wanted to know whether a sorted slice was worth using when the keys were short and the dictionary had only a dozen or so entries. With a larger dictionary, how much lookup time could a hash table built specifically for these keys save? I tested three implementations on the same keys, using a sorted slice, a custom hash table with linear probing, and a Go map. At 16, 1,024, and 16,384 keys, Go’s map was the fastest on successful lookups, both when looking up one key repeatedly and when cycling through different keys. That’s why go-intl kept map[string]int.

Say a dictionary contains four messages and "screen.ready" is at index 2. With a Go map, index["screen.ready"] gives us that 2 directly.

A sorted slice keeps the keys in lexical order. In this example the messages sit in the same order, so a key’s position in the slice is also its message index.

It has been revealed that binary search compares the middle key and uses that ordering to narrow the range. For instance, "screen.copy" sorts before "screen.ready", so we can discard it and everything to its left. The first key equal to the target is keys[2].

Figure 4. slices.BinarySearch finds the first key greater than or equal to the target, then checks for equality. The diagram omits the shared prefix screen..

Industry observers note that for the custom hash table, I used FNV-1a hashing and linear probing. With the same four keys, the experiment builds a table with eight slots. A key’s hash determines its starting slot. Each occupied slot stores the message index plus one, leaving 0 to mark an empty slot. Both "screen.copy" and "screen.ready" start at slot 4. We insert "screen.copy" first, so "screen.ready" takes the next slot, 5. Here’s the lookup for "screen.ready".

Sources indicate that stepping through successive slots after a collision is called linear probing. Reaching an empty slot before finding the key tells us the key is absent.

It has been revealed that figure 5. Linear probing takes us from slot 4 to slot 5. The stored value there is 3, so the message index is 3 − 1 = 2.

Industry observers note that the table shows how long it took to find the integer index for a message key, in nanoseconds per lookup (ns/op). Lower values are faster. Every lookup was a hit. The figures are medians from three runs on an Apple M3 Pro with Go 1.27.1.

Most of the changes described above happen before the map lookup or after the message has been retrieved.

As soon as the translation file is loaded, we know which text is literal, where the arguments go, and where each branch ends. We can keep all of that. Once a request has a language, the forty strings on the page can share it, too.

What has to wait until display time is the user’s name, how many items are in the cart, and how the number should appear.

That leaves each message with just the steps it needs at display time. For Ready, return the stored text. For Hello, Ada!, look up the name and concatenate the pieces. For 7 items, choose the wording based on the quantity, then write the number.

Why a Receivables Increase Can Break Your Cash Flow Reconciliation

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cash flow reconciliation can look correct while its input signs are wrong.
  • Industry observers note that the complication is that a filing may present a cash flow adjustment directly, while another dataset gives you the change in an asset balance.
  • For a small reconciliation, distinguish at least these fields:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A cash flow reconciliation can look correct while its input signs are wrong. Consider a synthetic example: net income is 100, depreciation is 20, and receivables rise by 15. Cash from operations is 105, not 135. Adding the receivables balance change as a positive adjustment reverses the working capital effect.

Industry observers note that the complication is that a filing may present a cash flow adjustment directly, while another dataset gives you the change in an asset balance. Those are different inputs. A rise in receivables is normally a negative adjustment in an indirect cash flow bridge, but an adjustment already reported as -15 must stay -15. Applying the same sign flip twice produces the wrong answer.

For a small reconciliation, distinguish at least these fields:.

Sources indicate that the following example uses invented numbers and deliberately excludes taxes, acquisitions, foreign exchange effects and other complications. All amounts are in millions of dollars for the same period.

The receivables increase reduces the bridge by 15; the payables increase adds 8. If the source already reports the receivables adjustment as -15, pass it as a reported_adjustment. Do not label it a balance_change.

In a recent development, this function handles only the sign convention for the specified inputs. It does not determine which accounts belong in operating cash flow. It also cannot turn every balance sheet movement into a cash flow adjustment.

Ending balance minus beginning balance includes movements that may have no operating cash effect. An acquired subsidiary can add receivables to the balance sheet on acquisition. Currency translation can change the reported balance of a foreign subsidiary. A reclassification can move an amount between line items. A cash flow statement may adjust for these effects when it presents changes in operating assets and liabilities.

For example, suppose receivables rise by 15 in total, including 5 acquired with a business. In a simplified case with no other effects, the operating receivables increase is 10 and the corresponding adjustment is -10. The raw balance change yields -15, leaving a 5 difference. That difference is a diagnostic lead, not proof that an acquisition explains a particular filing.

Use the cash flow statement and its notes to investigate. Retain the filing accession and the exact source for each reported adjustment. For a computed balance change, retain both balance dates and their source accessions. This lets a reviewer identify whether a mismatch comes from sign handling or from a movement outside the operating bridge.

It has been revealed that cash flows are duration facts; balance sheet amounts are instant facts. To compare them, the opening and closing balances must correspond to the cash flow period. A six-month cash flow figure paired with a three-month balance change will leave a residual even if both inputs are correct.

Match the reporting entity, currency, units and consolidation scope too. A segment receivables balance is not interchangeable with a consolidated cash flow adjustment. Check whether a value is a reported line item or a derived change before normalizing signs, and keep that classification in the stored record.

In a recent development, finally, compute a residual: reported operating cash flow minus net income and all included adjustments. A zero residual tells you the selected numbers add up; it does not establish that each line was classified correctly. A nonzero residual can reflect omitted lines, rounding, period mismatches or the noncash movements described above. Keep it visible instead of silently forcing the bridge to balance.

According to recent reports, the SEC's EDGAR API documentation describes the organization facts data and its scope. The original filing remains the place to inspect presentation and notes when an extracted fact lacks the context needed to explain a movement. For a related period matter, see normalizing discrete and year-to-date durations.

In a recent development, the gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

In a recent development, here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

In a recent development, the gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

According to recent reports, this limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:.

In a recent development, the IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:.

According to recent reports, the annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Vital sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclosure: We built and maintain all five Actors listed below under the publicrecords account on Apify.

A typical research or lead-qualification agent still has to leave the chat to answer five basic questions: what is this website built with, is this phone number even valid, what does Wikipedia say, what is the paper behind this DOI, and what do the domain's DNS, MX, SPF, and DMARC records look like?

We just published five single-purpose Actors on the Apify Store for those jobs. You can run them from the Store, call them over the Apify API, or pin them on Apify's hosted MCP server (https://mcp.apify.com) so Claude, Cursor, or any MCP client can use them directly.

Each Actor has a ready-to-run public task on its Store page if you want to try the prefilled example first.

Tech Stack Detector takes a list of website URLs or bare domains and returns what each site is built with: CMS, ecommerce platform, frameworks, analytics, ad pixels, marketing tools, payments, CDN and hosting, web server, and email provider. Every match includes a category, a confidence level, and the evidence that triggered it.

Public task on the Actor page: allbirds-techcrunch-vercel-stack.

You get one row per site, with fields such as domain, httpStatus, title, technologyNames, ecommerce, analytics, payments, cdnAndHosting, emailProvider, and a technologies list (name, category, confidence, version, evidence). A run on allbirds.com, for example, returns Shopify, Cloudflare, Google Tag Manager, Apple Pay, and Microsoft 365, each with the header, HTML, or DNS evidence behind it.

Phone Number Validator validates and formats phone numbers against the numbering proposal. It returns whether each number is valid or possible, plus E.164 and national forms, country, calling code, and line type.

This is a format and numbering-strategy check, not a live carrier, TCPA, or WhatsApp registration lookup.

Public task on the Actor page: validate-us-uk-au-phone-numbers.

Use phone_extract when the numbers are still inside a block of text rather than a clean list.

Sources indicate that wikipedia Search searches Wikipedia and returns article titles, URLs, last-edited timestamps, and intro extracts, with the CC BY-SA licence line on each row. Turn on full-article mode when you need the page text instead of the intro. The same Actor can also fetch ECB euro reference exchange rates or a U.S. Treasury par yield curve from those official public sources.

Logistics MX Record Drift Control With 4 Checks for Idempotent Domain Provisioning
